name: Archaeological Site of Leptis Magna
subtitle: A cultural property on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1982.

facts.label: In Danger
facts.value: on UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger (since 2016)

parts.text: UNESCO describes the property in these words: “Leptis Magna was enlarged and embellished by Septimius Severus, who was born there and later became emperor. It was one of the most beautiful cities of the Roman Empire, with its imposing public monuments, harbour, market-place, storehouses, shops and residential districts.”
Leptis Magna was a city of the Carthaginian Empire and of Roman Libya, at the mouth of the Wadi Lebda on the Mediterranean. Wikipedia says it was a Punic settlement before 500 BC.

It grew under Emperor Septimius Severus, who ruled from 193 to 211 and was born there. It fell to the Vandals in 439, rejoined the Eastern Empire in 533, and was abandoned after the Muslim conquest, around 647.
The article says that the city lay buried under sand dunes, which preserved it, until Italian archaeologists unearthed it in the 1920s during the Italian occupation of Libya.

gaps: The state of the site after the conflicts in Libya since 2011, which the part of the article read here does not reach.
